title: FastVGGT: Fast Visual Geometry Transformer
one_liner: Prune redundant tokens in visual transformers to run 4x faster on long image sequences without retraining.
lead: A vision transformer (a neural network that reads images as small patches) processes long video sequences to figure out where objects are in 3D space. On 1000 images, it becomes extremely slow because each image gets split into many tokens (small pieces), and the model wastes computation asking where each token should look. FastVGGT speeds this up 4 times by intelligently dropping the tokens that do redundant work, keeping only the ones that measure something new.

paras: Vision transformers process sequences of camera images to understand where objects sit in 3D space and how they move. On short sequences (say, 10 images), they work fine. But on 1000 images — a real video — they hit a wall: memory runs out, and computation crawls. A beginner's first try is simple: just feed all 1000 images in, same as 10 images. It fails because the transformer's scoring layer (which decides which past image regions matter for each small piece) compares every token from every image to every other token from every image. With 1000 images times 1000 tokens per image, that is 1 million tokens total. Comparing every token to every other token creates 1 million squared comparisons — 1 trillion scoring operations. Even one forward pass takes hours.

callout.html: Many tokens use the same scoring pattern to look at nearly identical regions, doing redundant work twice.

steps.text: Measure which tokens attend to nearly identical image regions.
Preserve all tokens from the first image as a stable global reference.
Retain tokens that look at rare or distinctive parts of the image.
Sample extra tokens randomly to ensure no area is completely missing.
Discard tokens that add no new information, cutting memory and computation.

paras: FastVGGT does not retrain the model or change its weights. Instead, it reduces the number of tokens (pieces of the image) fed into attention at each time step. Fewer tokens mean fewer comparisons, which means faster answers.

hidden.h2: Token redundancy: when two tokens watch the same thing
hidden.name: token attention overlap
paras: In the original transformer, each token outputs a list of scores showing where in prior frames it wants to look. If two tokens output nearly identical scores, they are looking at nearly the same regions and doing redundant work. FastVGGT estimates this overlap by comparing the attention scores (the look-at lists) of nearby tokens. Tokens with high overlap are marked as redundant.

The paper does not explicitly name a single formula for overlap, but the mechanism is clear: tokens whose attention patterns are nearly identical are pruned, while those with unique patterns are kept.

heat.caption: Darker means a token's attention pattern is unique; lighter means redundant.

reads.html: A token is redundant if it looks at the same places as neighboring tokens.
Global attention exhibits token collapse: many tokens converge to identical or near-identical attention patterns across frames.

mechanism.h2: Why pruning redundant tokens speeds everything up
paras: The bottleneck is the scoring layer computation: how many times do we ask 'where should this token look?' The answer depends on how many tokens exist. With 1 million tokens, that question is asked 1 trillion times. If we prune down to 250k tokens (one quarter), the question is asked only 62.5 billion times — 16 times fewer, because each token is scored against all prior tokens, so cutting the token count cuts the scoring operations by the same fraction. But there is a catch: pruning must preserve the information that the model needs to track object positions correctly. If we drop all tokens from frame 2, we lose the position and shape information from that frame. FastVGGT preserves frame 1 as an anchor (so the first reference stays constant), keeps salient tokens (tokens that look at unusual or important parts), and adds random spatial samples (so no region is entirely missing). This three-part strategy works because frame 1 gives a stable baseline, salient tokens catch changes in important regions, and random sampling fills gaps. The result is that position information stays intact even though most tokens are dropped.

stages.s: Measure score-pattern overlap between neighboring tokens
Mark tokens as redundant if overlap is high
Apply three-part strategy: anchor frame 1, keep salient, random-sample rest
250k tokens, faster scoring because fewer comparisons, position accurate because key tokens kept

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 12 tokens in one image. Frame 1 contributes 4 tokens (all kept). Remaining 8 tokens are checked: token-5 has saliency 0.8 (above tau=0.5, kept), token-6 has saliency 0.3 (below tau, dropped), token-7 saliency 0.7 (kept), token-8 saliency 0.2 (dropped). That is 3 + 2 = 5 salient tokens kept. Then random grid sampling adds 2 more tokens from blank regions. Total: 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 tokens kept out of 12. Pruning ratio = 8/12 = 67%, or 33% reduction.

math.note: The formula shows that frame 1 is always kept, high-uniqueness tokens are always kept, and random coverage fills gaps.

bars.h2: Speedup and error on long sequences

charts.title: Naive: feed all tokens
charts.note: Computation grows; error increases because small mistakes accumulate over long sequences.

charts.title: FastVGGT: prune redundant tokens
charts.note: Speeds up without error growth because key position landmarks stay intact and frame 1 anchors the whole sequence.

items.html: If tau is too strict, even important tokens are dropped. The position estimates become sparse and incomplete.
If the spatial grid is too coarse, large regions have no tokens. The model misses position and shape information in those areas.
If camera motion is large, frame 1 alone may not anchor the sequence. The model's position estimates drift over time.

items.b: Salient and redundant confuse each other.
items.html: A token can look at a common region in a unique way (e.g., first to detect a moving object). Overlap-based pruning might drop it.
Set tau carefully (e.g., via validation on short sequences), ensure random sampling covers all quadrants, and test on sequences with large camera motion to verify frame 1 anchors positions correctly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple tracking task: track the 3D position of a moving cube through a 100-frame video. (a) Run the original model (or a simple baseline) and record speed and final position error (how far the predicted position is from the true position). (b) Apply FastVGGT pruning (keep frame 1, keep tokens with saliency above 0.5, sample random grid every 4 by 4 pixels) and re-run with the exact same weights. (c) Confirm that speed increases at least 2x on 100 frames and error does not grow by more than 5%. On longer sequences (500 frames), the speedup should approach 4x. The speed gain comes from fewer tokens being scored against each other. The accuracy stays the same because frame 1 provides a stable baseline, salient tokens capture changes in key regions, and random sampling ensures no blind spots.
demo.metric_eq: speedup = time_naive divided by time_pruned, position_error = distance from predicted position to true position
demo.closing: The core insight is visible: pruning redundant tokens cuts computation, but strategy keeps position output correct.
